sentences.text: Sarcoprion is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish that lived during the Late Permian in Greenland.
Its jaws featured an arching row of connected teeth known as a tooth whorl, alongside flattened rectangular teeth in other parts of its mouth.
The most complete specimen possesses a skull and lower jaws nearly 90 cm long, with the total animal length estimated at up to 6 meters by John A. Long.
The name Sarcoprion derives from Greek roots meaning "flesh" and "saw".
The species name edax translates to "gluttonous".
The first four fossils of Sarcoprion edax were discovered in the 1930s by Eigil Nielsen in the Foldvik Creek Formation of East Greenland.
Eigil Nielsen hypothesized that Sarcoprion was likely unable to close its mouth based on skull and jaw reconstructions.
Nielsen suggested that rows of flattened pavement teeth along the mouth's lateral surfaces likely served as armor for the snout rather than for feeding.
Nielsen, Oleg Lebedev, and Wayne Itano have hypothesized that Sarcoprion used its tooth whorls like scissors to cut prey.
Oleg Lebedev proposed in 2009 that Sarcoprion ate fish and cephalopods, comparing its features to living toothed whales like sperm whales.
John Long speculated that Sarcoprion had a generalist diet including other cartilaginous fish and hard-shelled cephalopods.
Sarcoprion is classified in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the subclass Holocephali.
The animal belongs to the family Helicoprionidae.
It is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
Some sources classify Sarcoprion in the family Agassizodontidae.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Sarcoprion as Helicoprionidae.
It is debated whether Sarcoprion is related to other eugeneodonts, though earlier hypotheses placing it in a separate group are no longer supported.
